meta.title: Who really said "Show me a hero and I'll write you a tragedy"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: F. Scott Fitzgerald did write this line — not in a novel, but in his private notebooks, published posthumously in The Crack-Up (1945).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Show me a hero and I'll write you a tragedy'?
meta.ogDescription: Traced to F. Scott Fitzgerald's own notebooks, published posthumously in The Crack-Up (1945) — verified, with the misattribution to Tender Is the Night debunked.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line appears among the aphorisms in Fitzgerald’s own notebooks, grouped by him under the heading “E” and published posthumously in The Crack-Up (1945), edited by his friend Edmund Wilson.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Show me a hero and I will write you a tragedy.
trail: Fitzgerald recorded the line in his private notebooks, kept until his death in 1940.
It reached print posthumously in The Crack-Up ↗ (1945), Edmund Wilson’s edited collection of Fitzgerald’s essays, letters, and notebook excerpts.
The citation is corroborated by Wikiquote’s Fitzgerald page ↗, which lists it under “Notebooks” with the same source.
It is sometimes wrongly sold or captioned as a line from Tender Is the Night, but it does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s page for that novel ↗.
source.excerptNote: The notebook text as printed in The Crack-Up reads “I will write you a tragedy” — the wording carried by both WIST and Wikiquote, which cite that 1945 edition. Popular circulation and quote-aggregator sites contract it to the “I’ll” form used as this page’s searched title.
source.rightsHolder: Estate of F. Scott Fitzgerald / New Directions Publishing Corp.
source.rightsNote: The line comes from The Crack-Up, first published in 1945 by New Directions — well after the 1931 cutoff for presumptive U.S. public domain — so it remains under copyright, held by Fitzgerald’s estate and his publisher.

author.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.heading: About F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.bio: Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald is best known for The Great Gatsby (1925) and Tender Is the Night (1934), novels that made him the chief chronicler of the Jazz Age. He also kept working notebooks of observations, overheard lines, and aphorisms, which his friend and literary executor Edmund Wilson gathered and published after Fitzgerald’s death in 1940.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The authorship isn’t in dispute, but the source is often garbled or omitted by quote-aggregator sites.

items.why: Some product listings and quote pages present the line as if it were dialogue or narration from Fitzgerald’s 1934 novel Tender Is the Night; it does not appear in the novel’s text, per Wikiquote’s compiled quotations from it ↗.

Most social-media and quote-image circulations of the line drop the source entirely, presenting it as a floating Fitzgerald aphorism with no citation, which obscures that it comes from a specific, identifiable book.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Fitzgerald’s own, from his notebooks as published in The Crack-Up (1945) ↗ — not from any of his novels.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Fitzgerald jotted this line among the numbered aphorisms of his private notebooks, not in a novel or published essay, and never saw it in print himself — it surfaced five years after his death when Edmund Wilson edited The Crack-Up (1945), a collection of Fitzgerald’s confessional essays, letters, and notebook excerpts.

The line has since taken on a life of its own: it gave its title to Lisa Belkin’s 2005 nonfiction book Show Me a Hero and the 2015 HBO miniseries adapted from it, both about the political battle over public housing desegregation in Yonkers, New York.
